result:
The proposed answer of 9 is wrong, so I reject it. The formula for k(n,p) is never proved (it is only "verified on multiple cases"), and a simple construction shows it is too small.

**Counterexample.** For any prime p, Fermat's little theorem gives p | x^p − x for every integer x. Hence p^n divides (x^p − x)^n for all integers x. Expanding, (x^p − x)^n = (−x)^n + (terms of higher degree), and the lowest-degree term is (−1)^n x^n. So the x^n coefficient is ±1. Multiplying by (−1)^n gives a polynomial with integer coefficients, x^n coefficient exactly 1, and value divisible by p^n at every integer. Therefore k(n,p) ≥ n.

**Contradiction with the proposed formula.** The solution claims k(11,11) = 1, but this construction gives k(11,11) ≥ 11. The claimed formula Σ⌊n/(p^i(p−1))⌋ is therefore false for these cases.

**Bound on the true sum.** Each k(n,p) is at least n, so the double sum is at least 2·(11+12+13+14+15) = 130. The proposed value of 9 is far below this.

VERDICT: REJECT
